# Numbers 3:27–51 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Passage

This section completes the census and organization of the Levite clans (vv. 27–39) and then records the exchange of the Levites for Israel's firstborn, including the redemption of the 273 "excess" firstborn with money (vv. 40–51).

---

## Verse 27

**v. 27: "From Kohath came the clans of the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites; these were the clans of the Kohathites."**

Kohath was the second son of Levi. His four sons gave their names to four Levitical clans. Among the Amramites were Moses and Aaron themselves (Exodus 6:20), making the Kohathites the kinsmen of the priestly family. Gill notes that the four Kohathite clans together were as numerous as both other branches of Levi's descendants combined. The Pulpit Commentary observes that this family "had many privileges above the others" — from them came Moses, Aaron, and all the priests; they had the chief place about the tabernacle and the care of the most holy things.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/3-27.htm

The Enduring Word commentary notes that the term "Amramites" reminds us of Aaron and Moses, but suggests that Amram may have been an ancestor rather than the direct father — "Aaron and Moses were from the family of Kohath, of the tribe of Levi" (Allen, cited by Guzik).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/

---

## Verse 28

**v. 28: "The number of all the males a month old or more was 8,600. They were responsible for the duties of the sanctuary."**

The Kohathites numbered 8,600 males — the largest of the three Levite branches. Gill comments that though they had double the number of families (four clans versus Gershon's two), their proportionate increase was not as large as might be expected. The phrase "keeping the charge of the sanctuary" (as older translations render it) means they had primary responsibility for the sanctuary's principal sacred objects. Gill notes that while infants of a month old could not literally perform these duties, the males were counted from that age because they would be "instructed and trained up from their youth" for this service.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/3-28.htm

**Scholarly/Textual note:** Several commentators (Wenham, Keil & Delitzsch, Constable) suggest the Kohathite number may originally have been 8,300, with the Hebrew letter for "3" (shin) being corrupted to "6" (samekh) in transmission. This would bring the Levite total (22,300) into line with the firstborn count.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-3.html

---

## Verse 29

**v. 29: "The clans of the Kohathites were to camp on the south side of the tabernacle."**

The south side was the position of honour, second only to the east (where Moses, Aaron, and the priests camped). Pett's Commentary calls this "the second most prestigious position." Gill notes this honour was fitting since one of their families (the Amramites) included the priests, and the Kohathites "had the more honourable charge, having the holy places and holy things committed to their care." Gill also observes that this positioning between the tabernacle and the camp of Reuben explains how Korah (a Kohathite) became so closely associated with Dathan and Abiram (Reubenites) in the rebellion of Numbers 16.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/numbers-3.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html

---

## Verse 30

**v. 30: "And the leader of the families of the Kohathites was Elizaphan son of Uzziel."**

Elizaphan (meaning "God has protected") was a grandson of Kohath through his youngest son Uzziel. Pett notes he was "chief over all the clans which were a part of the sub-tribe." The Enduring Word commentary highlights that some Kohathites, "under the rebellious leadership of Korah, would later challenge the authority of Moses and Aaron" (Numbers 16) — making the orderly chain of command established here all the more significant.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/numbers-3.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/

---

## Verse 31

**v. 31: "Their duties were the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the articles of the sanctuary used with them, and the curtain—all the service for these items."**

This verse lists the most sacred items of the tabernacle entrusted to the Kohathites. Gill identifies each: the ark with the mercy seat (in the Most Holy Place); the table of showbread, the golden lampstand, and the altar of incense (in the Holy Place); and the altar of burnt offering (in the court). "The hanging" (or "screen") is interpreted by Jarchi (cited by Gill) as the veil dividing the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place — distinct from the other hangings which were the responsibility of the Gershonites.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html

Barnes' Notes observes: "Of the Levites, the Kohathites, the kinsmen of Moses and Aaron, and the most numerous, have the most important charge confided to them, namely, that of the ark, the altars, and the more especially sacred furniture generally."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/numbers-3.html

Pett adds a sobering note: the Kohathites "would, however, never see them 'uncovered.' Always the priest would have covered them" — a point developed in Numbers 4, where the Kohathites are warned not to touch or even look upon the holy things lest they die.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/numbers-3.html

---

## Verse 32

**v. 32: "The chief of the leaders of the Levites was Eleazar son of Aaron the priest; he oversaw those responsible for the duties of the sanctuary."**

Eleazar, Aaron's surviving eldest son (after Nadab and Abihu's deaths) and future high priest, was appointed "prince of the princes" — chief over the three Levite chieftains (Eliasaph of Gershon, Elizaphan of Kohath, Zuriel of Merari). Gill notes Eleazar had particular oversight of the Kohathites because the items they carried were those the priests had a special concern with (see Numbers 4:32). Pett observes: "The importance of the task of the Kohathites is evidenced by the mention here of Eleazar."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/numbers-3.html

---

## Verse 33

**v. 33: "From Merari came the clans of the Mahlites and Mushites; these were the Merarite clans."**

Merari was Levi's third son, and his two sons (Mahli and Mushi) produced the two Merarite clans. Gill notes these were the smallest branch in terms of families (only two), matching Gershon.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html

---

## Verse 34

**v. 34: "The number of all the males a month old or more was 6,200."**

The Merarites numbered 6,200 — the smallest of the three Levite divisions. Together with the Gershonites (7,500) and Kohathites (8,600), the raw total is 22,300.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html

---

## Verse 35

**v. 35: "The leader of the families of the Merarites was Zuriel son of Abihail; they were to camp on the north side of the tabernacle."**

Zuriel ("my rock is God") was appointed chief of the Merarites. The north side placed them between the tabernacle and the camp of Dan.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/

---

## Verses 36–37

**vv. 36–37: "The duties assigned to the sons of Merari were the tabernacle's frames, crossbars, posts, bases, and all its equipment…as well as the posts of the surrounding courtyard with their bases, tent pegs, and ropes."**

The Merarites were responsible for the structural "hardware" of the tabernacle: the acacia wood boards (frames), crossbars, pillars, silver bases (sockets), bronze bases for the court pillars, tent pegs, and ropes. Enduring Word notes this was "difficult and important work." The tabernacle's structural components were covered with precious metals, and the estimated weight was approximately 19,000 pounds (8,600+ kilograms). Because of the heavy loads, the Merarites were given more ox-carts than the Gershonites (Numbers 7:6–8), while the Kohathites received none since they carried the holy items on their shoulders.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html

Constable's Expository Notes sums up the three branches memorably:

| Group | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Gershonites | "software" (curtains and coverings) |
| Kohathites | "furniture and utensils" |
| Merarites | "hardware" (boards and bars) |

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-3.html

---

## Verse 38

**v. 38: "Moses, Aaron, and Aaron's sons were to camp to the east of the tabernacle, toward the sunrise, before the Tent of Meeting. They were to perform the duties of the sanctuary as a service on behalf of the Israelites; but any outsider who approached the sanctuary was to be put to death."**

The east side, facing the sunrise, was the most honoured position — directly before the entrance to the tabernacle. Allen (cited in Enduring Word) notes: "The morning sun would shine first on the entrance of the Holy Place, as a symbol of the life-giving light of God that illumines the place of his presence."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/

The phrase "any outsider who approached" (Hebrew *zar* — stranger, unauthorized person) carried the death penalty. This "outsider" could be a non-Israelite, a non-Levite Israelite, or even a Levite who presumed to do priestly work. Enduring Word comments: "This old covenant emphasized a sense of exclusion; the new covenant emphasizes inclusion" — yet even in the new covenant, God has appointed order and offices.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/

---

## Verse 39

**v. 39: "The total number of Levites that Moses and Aaron counted by their clans at the LORD's command, including all the males a month old or more, was 22,000."**

The stated total (22,000) differs from the sum of the three clans (7,500 + 8,600 + 6,200 = 22,300). Barnes' Notes presents two traditional explanations: (1) the extra 300 were firstborn Levites who, being already dedicated to God, could not serve as substitutes for firstborn Israelites from other tribes; (2) the difference is due to a textual corruption, with the Kohathite number originally being 8,300 (Hebrew *shin* = 3 being misread as *samekh* = 6).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/numbers-3.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/

---

## Verse 40

**v. 40: "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Number every firstborn male of the Israelites a month old or more, and list their names.'"**

This command flows directly from the principle established in Numbers 3:11–13: God claimed Israel's firstborn at the Passover, and now the Levites would serve as their substitutes. The census of firstborn males (one month and older) was needed to establish the exchange. As Enduring Word notes: "There can be a difference between what God lays claim to and what He materially receives."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary

---

## Verse 41

**v. 41: "You are to take the Levites for Me—I am the LORD—in place of all the firstborn of Israel, and the livestock of the Levites in place of all the firstborn of the livestock of the Israelites."**

This verse declares the grand substitution: the tribe of Levi takes the place of all firstborn Israelites (both human and animal). The phrase "I am the LORD" underscores divine authority. Precept Austin quotes Currid: "The Levites and their cattle, therefore, release the firstborn of Israel from sacred status and from the duty of the service of the sanctuary." The Levites became "living substitutionary sacrifices."

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary

Gill explains that the Levites' cattle were not given to the priests but remained with the Levites for their support, since the Levites themselves were now dedicated to God's service.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html

---

## Verses 42–43

**vv. 42–43: "So Moses numbered all the firstborn of the Israelites, as the LORD had commanded him. The total number of the firstborn males a month old or more, listed by name, was 22,273."**

The census yielded 22,273 firstborn males. Compared with 22,000 Levites, there was an excess of 273. Barnes' Notes observes this number is remarkably small compared to the total male population of 603,550 (Numbers 2:32) — the normal proportion would be roughly one in four. The explanation is that only those firstborn *since the Exodus* were counted (i.e., those born after God claimed the firstborn at Passover, about thirteen months earlier). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown likewise says: "The only way of accounting for it is, by supposing those firstborn only were counted…which had been born since the departure from Egypt."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/numbers-3.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/numbers/3.htm

---

## Verses 44–45

**vv. 44–45: "Again the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, 'Take the Levites in place of all the firstborn of Israel, and the livestock of the Levites in place of their livestock. The Levites belong to Me; I am the LORD.'"**

The command is repeated for emphasis and clarity. As Pett notes: "Yahweh now repeats His instruction, stressing its importance, and making it crystal clear." The cattle exchange was done "in the gross" (Barnes) — not head for head — since the Levites' livestock as a whole substituted for the firstborn cattle of all Israel.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/numbers-3.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/numbers-3.html

---

## Verses 46–47

**vv. 46–47: "To redeem the 273 firstborn Israelites who outnumber the Levites, you are to collect five shekels for each one, according to the sanctuary shekel of twenty gerahs."**

The 273 "excess" firstborn could not be matched to a Levite, so they had to be redeemed with money. The rate of five shekels per person corresponded to the valuation of a male child under five years old in Leviticus 27:6. The "sanctuary shekel" was the standard weight kept at the sanctuary — the parenthetical note that it was "twenty gerahs" distinguished it from other shekel standards in use. The Cambridge Bible explains: this was "the ancient Hebrew-Phoenician shekel," weighing about 224.6 grains; at the time the text was written, secular commerce used a heavier Persian-Babylonian shekel.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/3-47.htm

---

## Verse 48

**v. 48: "Give the money to Aaron and his sons as the redemption price for the excess among the Israelites."**

The redemption money was paid to Aaron and his sons. Gill explains the logic: since the Levites were given to the priests in lieu of the firstborn (who originally belonged to God and would have served the sanctuary), and there was a shortfall of 273 Levites, it was just that the redemption price for the shortfall also go to the priests as compensation.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html

**Who paid?** The text does not specify how the 273 families were determined. Jewish tradition (recorded by Jarchi and the Talmud, Sanhedrin 17a, and cited by Gill and JFB) says it was decided by lot: Moses wrote "a son of Levi" on 22,000 slips and "five shekels" on 273 slips; each firstborn drew a slip. The Pulpit Commentary suggests the money was exacted from the parents of the most recently born. Whedon's Commentary proposes it was a tax paid from a common tribal fund.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/numbers/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-3.html

---

## Verses 49–50

**vv. 49–50: "So Moses collected the redemption money from those in excess of the number redeemed by the Levites. He collected the money from the firstborn of the Israelites: 1,365 shekels, according to the sanctuary shekel."**

Moses carried out the command exactly. The arithmetic is straightforward: 273 × 5 = 1,365 shekels. Gill calculates this as about 170 pounds in 18th-century English money (roughly £170). The Pulpit Commentary and Enduring Word note that this silver was "redemption money" — the price that freed the excess firstborn from their obligation to God.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/

---

## Verse 51

**v. 51: "And Moses gave the redemption money to Aaron and his sons in obedience to the word of the LORD, just as the LORD had commanded him."**

The verse closes the section by emphasizing Moses' exact obedience. The Pulpit Commentary notes the money was "doubtless applied to the support of the tabernacle worship." The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge cross-references this with 1 Samuel 12:3–4 and Acts 20:33, where Samuel and Paul each declare they have taken nothing from the people unjustly — a contrast to faithful stewardship.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tsk/numbers-3.html

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### The "Total Depravity" and "Substitution" Emphasis (Reformed / Presbyterian)

Reformed commentators see in this passage a vivid picture of substitutionary atonement. Precept Austin quotes the ESV Study Bible note: "After the golden calf incident, the Levites took the place of the firstborn boys (Ex. 32:25–29)." The entire exchange — Levites for firstborn, cattle for cattle, silver for the excess — is read as foreshadowing Christ's substitutionary death. Allen (cited in Enduring Word) notes the Hebrew phrase "instead of" serves as "a clear example of substitution in the Hebrew Scriptures (cf. Genesis 22:13: 'a ram…instead of his son'; cf. also Matthew 20:28)."

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/

### Baptist / Spurgeon Tradition

Baptist commentators (Gill being a leading Reformed Baptist voice) tend to emphasise the sovereignty of God in choosing the Levites: "this was his own act and deed, and which he did of his own will and pleasure, who is a sovereign Being." Gill also addresses the old Jewish and Christian notion that firstborn had served as family priests before the Levitical system, noting the evidence for this is thin — "it does not appear, before the fixing the priesthood in Aaron's family, that the firstborn in a family were priests."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-3.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

Guzik emphasises the practical application for the new covenant believer: the old covenant stressed exclusion ("the outsider who comes near shall be put to death"), while the new covenant stresses inclusion — every believer is a priest (1 Peter 2:5, 9). Yet Guzik also stresses that God still appoints order in the church, and "honoring those boundaries…reflects our respect for God's design." He also highlights that the Levites served as "spiritual security" — a role "more like a policeman shooting a bank robber" (Wenham) than the gentle picture often imagined.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-3/

### Anglican / Broad Evangelical (Cambridge Bible, Pulpit Commentary)

The older Anglican-influenced commentaries focus on textual and historical details. The Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges gives careful attention to weights and measures: the sanctuary shekel as distinct from the Persian-Babylonian shekel, the gerah equivalent to the Greek obolus. The Pulpit Commentary stresses the practical justice of the arrangement: the redemption money compensated Aaron for the missing Levites who would have served him.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/3.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/3.htm

### Lutheran (Where Found)

No specific Lutheran commentary on this passage was retrievable from lcms.org or 1517.org within the search scope. Lutheran exegesis would typically be expected to emphasise the distinction between Law (the detailed regulations, the death penalty for outsiders) and Gospel (the substitution pointing to Christ), a reading broadly shared with Reformed traditions.

---

## Other Views

### Modern / Critical Scholarship

The NET Bible notes highlight the technical formula "Now these are the generations" (*toledot*) that opens Numbers 3, connecting it to the structuring of Genesis. They also observe that the expression "fill the hand" (ordain) was known in Mesopotamia and likely originated from placing a symbol of office in the ordinand's hands — "less likely is Noth's suggestion that it derives from money being placed into a priest's hands as payment."

The textual discrepancy between 22,000 and 22,300 is widely noted by critical scholars (Wenham, Keil & Delitzsch, Noordtzij) as a "copyist's error" in verse 28.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-3-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-3.html

### Catholic Reading

Catholic resources (newadvent.org, catholic.com) were not directly accessible for this specific passage within the available searches. The Catholic tradition, following the Fathers, would typically read the Levitical priesthood as prefiguring the ordained priesthood of the New Covenant and the redemption money as a type of the price Christ paid. The Haydock commentary (available on studylight.org but not fetched) would be the standard traditional Catholic source.

### Orthodox Reading

No specific Orthodox commentary on this passage was retrievable from oca.org within the search scope.

### Prosperity / Word of Faith Teaching

No specific prosperity-gospel interpretation of this passage was found in the searched sources. A typical application in this tradition might focus on the redemption money as establishing a "law of exchange" (silver for souls), but this could not be verified from the permitted sites.

### Summary of the Traditional Reading

Across virtually all traditions consulted, the passage is understood as establishing the divinely ordered organization of the Levites for tabernacle service and the principle of substitution: the Levites take the place of the firstborn whom God claimed at Passover. The 273 excess firstborn are redeemed with silver at five shekels per head, paid to the priests. The passage teaches God's holiness (the death penalty for unauthorized approach), His sovereignty in choosing servants, the importance of order in worship, and the principle that redemption requires a price — whether a substitute (the Levites) or silver. Christian interpreters across traditions see in this a foreshadowing of Christ's substitutionary redemption.
